days.title: Day 1 – Introduction to HTML
days.definition: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language for creating web pages and web applications. It describes the structure of web pages using markup.
days.explanation:
HTML is like the skeleton of a website. It provides the basic structure that is then enhanced and modified by CSS and JavaScript. HTML uses tags like

,

,

to define elements such as headings, paragraphs, and divisions. These elements tell the browser how to display the content. Think of HTML as the building blocks of web pages - without it, there would be no structure to display text, images, or links on the web.

News websites use HTML for articles, e-commerce sites use it for product listings, and social media platforms use it to display posts and comments.

days.title: Day 2 – HTML Editors and Setup
days.definition: HTML editors are software tools used to create and edit HTML code, ranging from simple text editors to sophisticated Integrated Development Environments (IDEs).
days.explanation: You can write HTML using any text editor, but specialized HTML editors make the process easier with features like syntax highlighting, code completion, and live preview. Basic editors like Notepad work fine for beginners, while advanced editors like VS Code or specialized tools like Dreamweaver provide powerful features. The most important thing is to save your files with the .html extension so browsers recognize them as web pages.

days.real_world_example: Professional web developers use editors like VS Code, Sublime Text, or WebStorm. These tools help manage large projects with multiple files, provide error checking, and integrate with version control systems like Git. Even simple tools like Notepad++ or online editors like CodePen are used for quick prototyping and learning.

days.title: Day 4 – HTML Attributes
days.definition: HTML attributes provide additional information about elements, modifying their behavior or appearance. They are always specified in the start tag.
days.explanation: Attributes add extra details to HTML elements. For example, the tag needs a 'src' attribute to specify the image source, and the tag needs an 'href' attribute to specify the link destination. Attributes usually come in name/value pairs like name="value". Some attributes are global (work on all elements) while others are specific to certain elements.

days.code_example:
Understanding Climate Change

Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns. These shifts may be natural, but since the 1800s, human activities have been the main driver of climate change.

Causes of Climate Change

The primary cause of climate change is the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas. This produces heat-trapping gases that are responsible for most of the warming observed in recent decades.

Deforestation, agriculture, and industrial processes also contribute to greenhouse gas emissions.

Greenhouse Gas Effect

Greenhouse gases trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere, much like the glass walls of a greenhouse.

Impacts of Climate Change

Climate change affects everything from weather patterns to sea levels, biodiversity, and human health.

Sea Level Rise

As temperatures rise, ice sheets and glaciers melt, contributing to sea level rise that threatens coastal communities.

Extreme Weather Events

Climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events like hurricanes, droughts, and heatwaves.

days.explanation: Links are what make the web a 'web' - they connect pages together. The <a> tag creates clickable links that can point to other web pages, files, email addresses, or specific locations within the same page. Links can be text, images, or other elements. days.title: Day 8 – Lists (Ordered, Unordered)
days.definition: HTML lists organize items in either ordered (numbered) or unordered (bulleted) formats, helping present information in a structured, readable way.
days.explanation: Lists are essential for presenting collections of related items. Unordered lists (<ul>) use bullets and are for items without a specific sequence. Ordered lists (<ol>) use numbers/letters and are for sequential items. Each list item uses the <li> tag. Lists can be nested to create hierarchies and are frequently used for navigation menus, instructions, features lists, and more.

days.title: Day 11 – Semantic HTML
days.definition: Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags that clearly describe their content and role, making web pages more accessible, SEO-friendly, and maintainable.
days.explanation: Semantic tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, and <footer> give meaning to the structure of a webpage. Unlike generic <div> tags, semantic elements tell both browsers and developers what kind of content they contain. This improves accessibility for screen readers, helps search engines understand page structure, and makes code easier to read and maintain.

days.title: Day 12 – HTML Entities and Symbols
days.definition: HTML entities are special codes used to display reserved characters, symbols, and characters not found on keyboards, ensuring they render correctly in browsers.
days.explanation: Since some characters have special meaning in HTML (like < and >), we use entities to display them. Entities also allow showing symbols like ©, €, or mathematical symbols. Entities start with & and end with ;. They're essential for displaying special characters correctly across different browsers and systems, and for ensuring HTML code doesn't break when it contains reserved characters.

days.title: Day 13 – HTML Formatting Elements
days.definition: HTML formatting elements apply specific text styles and meanings to content, such as bold, italic, emphasized, or marked text, without using CSS.
days.explanation: Formatting elements give semantic meaning or visual emphasis to text. While CSS is preferred for visual styling, HTML formatting elements convey meaning. For example, <strong> indicates importance, while <b> just makes text bold. <em> indicates emphasis, while <i> just makes text italic. Understanding when to use each element helps create semantically correct and accessible content.

days.title: Day 16 – HTML Head Elements
days.definition: The HTML head section contains meta-information about the document, including its title, character set, styles, scripts, and other metadata that isn't displayed on the page.
days.explanation: The <head> element is a container for metadata about the HTML document. It's placed between <html> and <body> tags. Following best practices makes your websites more accessible, faster, easier to maintain, and compatible across different browsers and devices. While browsers often render invalid HTML, validation helps prevent unpredictable behavior and improves quality.

days.title: Day 18 – HTML and CSS Integration
days.definition: HTML provides structure while CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation. Integrating both creates visually appealing, well-structured web pages.
days.explanation: HTML defines what content is on a page, while CSS defines how it looks. They work together like a house: HTML is the structure (walls, rooms), CSS is the decoration (paint, furniture). CSS can be added inline within HTML elements, internally in the <style> tag, or externally in separate .css files. Understanding how to integrate CSS with HTML is essential for creating modern, responsive, and attractive websites.
days.code_example:
HTML and CSS Integration Methods

Three ways to combine HTML structure with CSS styling

1. Inline CSS (style attribute)

CSS added directly to HTML elements using the style attribute.

Example:

<p style="color: blue; font-size: 16px;">
  This text is styled with inline CSS.
</p>

Pros: Quick, specific to element

Cons: Hard to maintain, not reusable

2. Internal CSS (<style> tag)

CSS added in the <head> section using <style> tags.

Example:

<style>
  .internal-example {
    color: green;
    font-weight: bold;
  }
</style>

<p class="internal-example">Styled with internal CSS</p>

Pros: Page-specific, better organization

Cons: Not reusable across pages

3. External CSS (separate .css file)

CSS in separate file linked with <link> tag.

Example:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

<p class="external-example">Styled with external CSS</p>

Pros: Reusable, cacheable, best practice

Cons: Extra HTTP request

days.title: Day 19 – Responsive Design Basics
days.definition: Responsive web design creates websites that adapt to different screen sizes and devices, providing optimal viewing experience on desktops, tablets, and mobile phones.
days.explanation: Responsive design uses flexible layouts, images, and CSS media queries to automatically adjust web pages to fit different screen sizes. With the variety of devices people use to access the web (phones, tablets, laptops, desktops), responsive design ensures your website looks good and works well everywhere. Key concepts include fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries that apply different CSS rules based on device characteristics.

Responsive Design Basics

This page adapts to different screen sizes

  • Home
  • About
  • Services
  • Portfolio

Why Responsive Design?

With the variety of devices used to access the web, responsive design ensures your website looks good and works well everywhere.

Key Principles

Fluid Grids

Use percentage-based widths instead of fixed pixels to create flexible layouts that adapt to screen size.

Flexible Images

Images scale within their containing elements using max-width: 100% to prevent overflow.

Media Queries

Apply different CSS rules based on device characteristics like width, height, and orientation.

Responsive Video Example
